question: What does Stripe CTO David Singleton recommend teams do to build better products?

S1.title: Building a culture of excellence | David Singleton (CTO of Stripe)
S1.text:
David Singleton (00:00:00):
The way we think about product development at Stripe, it really is to find the correct set of early users to kind of co-create the product with. Maybe the best example of that is Stripe billing. When we got to starting the Stripe billing product, we realized that there were a number of our existing users, these were companies like Figma and Slack, were already using Stripe for payments, but had these subscriptions business models. And we figured that there were going to be many more of these kind of companies into the future. And we could see that they were really kind of pushing the boundaries of what was possible here.

(00:00:32):
So we decided to co-create the product with them. So we had shared Slack channels, we'd actually show them product on a very regular basis, get their feedback on it. And only when that original kind of Alpha group was super, super happy with the product did we then think it might be ready to go to a broader audience. So that is just how we build product at Stripe. And that means that every engineer building product at Stripe really has many of the kind of attributes and will exercise many of the attributes that'll you often find in PMs in other companies.

answer.summary: Singleton recommends deeply understanding users, co-creating with a carefully chosen group of early users, and repeatedly checking the product from a specific user’s perspective before expanding or shipping. He also emphasizes engineers taking product ownership and teams sweating details at high-friction moments.

sections.heading: Co-create with the right early users
sections.content: Find users whose needs are pushing the problem forward, learn their challenges and goals, and bring them into a shared development loop. For Stripe Billing, the team worked with existing Stripe customers such as Figma and Slack, showed them the product regularly through shared Slack channels, and gathered feedback. Singleton says they waited until the original alpha group was very happy before considering a broader release.

sections.heading: Make product work part of everyone’s job
sections.content: For developer-focused products, Singleton says strong product work combines technical understanding with user insight and strategy. Stripe expected early team members—and product-building engineers—to get to know users well and bring those insights into product development, exercising attributes often associated with product managers.

sections.heading: Find and address friction from the user’s perspective
sections.content: Use friction logging: clearly identify the particular user you are modeling, then go through the product in that user’s shoes and record points of friction. Reviews can be done asynchronously, or as a group walkthrough with the product team and cross-functional partners such as support and executives; participants can log issues during the walkthrough and discuss afterward which need addressing. Singleton’s example of meticulousness is API error messages that link directly to the documentation explaining how to solve the problem.
